4. The workshop (a) communicates to the east with the small room directly attached to it (b), bordered by a white marble threshold, now no longer visible, and also open towards the atrium (c) through the window in the background, and with the corridor (d).

5. Bottega (a), wall S: the destructive action of atmospheric agents does not allow the partitions of the decoration to be distinguished, in which the central panel is yellow and the side panels are red. In panel E you can see the traces of a rectangular square; the upper white area was adorned with thyrsis, swans, candelabra and other motifs typical of the IV style.  79 N54733

7. Backroom (b), S wall: in section E there remains a short segment of the edge of the corolla carpet (?) that framed the panels, in which there were vignettes of cupids, separated by the central compartment.

6. The back room (b) was covered with a vault, as can be guessed from the presence of the lunette on the N wall, painted in the fourth style according to a bipartite structure scheme of which we still see the proportions, while the colors are completely lost. The curved stucco frame features a lotus motif and palmettes on symmetrical scrolls lying down.

8. Atrium (c): the collapse of the wall E, separating it from the viridarium (h) gives the impression that it is a single room, while the atrium ended in correspondence with the large window open towards the entrance hall at no. 8 which was thus illuminated. The walls were covered with a high plinth of cocciopesto; the mouth of the cistern opened into the floor. '79 N54696
9. Corridor (d), N wall distinguished from that of the workshop by the slight overhang of the masonry pillar and the change of decorative part.

10. Corridor (d), S wall: although discolored, the plaster shows in the upper part, under the holes in the housing of the beams of a mezzanine, the traces of painted horizontal bands, a residue of the "rough ornaments" visible at the time of discovery. 79 N54692

11. Kitchen (e): the narrow service area, located on the S side of the house, allowed you to exit from the post office of number 8, visible in the background, and could be reached from the atrium (c), whose entrance is visible on the right. The presence of an upper floor is evident in the door above the one on the O wall and in the niche of the latrine with terracotta pipes visible on the S wall.

12. Tablinum (g), wall N: the small strips of painted plaster retain traces of a carpet border and a narrow compartment with a thin metal candelabrum in the white middle area, above the yellow plinth with aquatic plants.

13. Viridarium (h): on the wall E there was a garden painting documented in the ink drawing by G. Abbate (cf. Disegnatori, p. 405, fig. 228). Birds rest on a marble fountain supported by the statue of a sphinx while on the sides there are two herons, recognizable by the tuft on their heads and the shape of their bodies. Two masks hang from above and in the plinth there was a representation of a Triton shooting an arrow at a sea panther already hit by a dart. Above there was a frieze with hunting scenes among animals: deer, bears, a lion, a panther and the group of a bull fighting with a lion, already very poorly preserved at the time of discovery, and probably for this reason not reproduced.
14. Viridarium (h): the E wall, disfigured by a large hole made by the ancients, in its current condition.

15. Viridarium (h), S wall, central section with a niche interrupted in the upper part by an ancient hole: above the red plinth there was the garden painting on a yellow background flanked by a statue of Heracles with a club and that of a Satyr playing the double flute. In the center of the garden itself there was a masonry basin with walls painted in red and with in the center, as a fountain jet, a marble trunk on which rested the statue of a cupid.

16. Viridarium (h), S wall, section W with the arched niche at the bottom of which are still visible traces of the purple plinth in front of which is placed a statue of Nymph as a fountain, holding a crater from which water flowed. In correspondence with the painted jet there was a hole for the actual escape of the water collected in the basin below; the bottom of the wall is blue.
17. Cubicle (i): cocciopesto floor with laVa threshold for a door with asymmetrical leaves and rectangular recesses for the jambs.

18. Cubicle (i), N wall: the red plinth is made up of panels separated by narrow compartments; the middle area is white with panels separated by architectural views closed at the bottom by red partitions surmounted by candelabra. In the central panel, framed by arched garlands and floral candelabra, there was the painting with Apollo seated on a rock, with his right hand resting on the corresponding knee and the lyra in his left; the side panels have staple carpet edges.

19. Cubicle (i), wall E: the compositional scheme is similar to that of wall N, with the panels of the middle area separated by architectural views with red partitions. In the central panel there was the painting (33 x 26 cm) with Ganymede.

20. Cubicle (i), wall E: the reproduction of the painting by N.La Volpe shows a woman languidly lying on the rocks, who turns her back to the viewer and raises her right hand upwards towards the eagle resting on the rocks. He evidently refers to the interpretation given also in the report of the PAH (20 May 1851, II, p. 503) which saw Danae in the figure stretched out. According to Minervini (Minervini, in BAN, I, p. 27) the bird of prey would hold in its claws the Phrygian cap of the one identified as Ganymede, a reading also followed by Aureli who, in pencil on cardboard (ADS 972: cfr. Disegnatori, p. 838, fig. 2), depicts an immature, short-haired young man in front of an eagle that does not have the majestic pride of this one drawn by La Volpe (cf. also Disegnatori, p. 727, fig. 193).
21. Cubicle (i), S wall with the door to the viridarium (h): the white panels retain traces of the edges of the staple carpet, outlined in red. 79 N54716

22. Cubicle (i), wall O: the architectural views that separate the panels of the middle area are extremely simple, especially in the lower part, which is the only one preserved. The painting of the central panel was already lost in 1851, the time of the discovery of this house.

23. Triclinium (k), wall N: the decoration of this room is in a simple IV style and rather heavy in the vertical subdivision of the wall in which the white and yellow of the middle area predominate over the red of the plinth. In this are the central panel with a square carpet border and the sides with plants separated by narrow compartments with a disc hanging from knotted bandages. In the middle area, in the center there is a stretched yellow carpet in front of which there was the painting of Achilles

1. Entrance hall (a): the walls of the room inclined towards the street, were in place on a frame with large mirrors of limestone stones, and covered in the fourth style with a high black plinth divided into panels by narrow red bands, while the upper area was white.

7. Triclinium (d): the painting with Selene and Endymion (MNN, inv. 9246) is also reproduced by G. Abbate (ADS 975, cf. Disegnatori, p. 407, fig. 229). The young man lying down and covered by the red mantle looks towards Selene who advances from above, with the crescent moon on his head and a scepter in his left, while with his right he holds the edge of the yellow mantle. Behind him emerges a circular base, also present in the painting with Narcissus (see fig. 9). In the side panel there was a vignette of a figure

8. Triclinium (d): another painting (MNN, inv. 9533, but erroneously indicated as 9532), described at the time of the discovery, before the detachment, was the one with Apollo and Daphne, also documented by drawings by G. Abbate (ADS 978 and 979, cf. Disegnatori, p. 407, figs. 230, 231). Apollo seated on a square boulder on which the great lyra is leaning, which therefore leaves no doubt to the identification of the subject, and partly covered by the bluish mantle, holds Daphne who flees to the left holding a flap of the red mantle that swells behind her legs for movement. An architectural backdrop, behind which a pillar protrudes, indicates an indoor setting of the scene that usually takes place outdoors. In the panel next to the painting there was a cartoon of a cupid with a bundle of herbs.

9. Triclinium (d): the third painting (MNN, inv. 9386) defined as "badly preserved" already at the time of its discovery, was however detached. It is yet another replica of Narcissus who is reflected in the fatal pond. In this copy, the figure of Eco is not relegated to a secondary position but, placed on the right and cloaked in yellow and blue, she offers a garland of flowers to the young man with whom she has fallen in love. Almost completely lost is the figure of the cupid with the torch turned upside down. The Above, who first described the painting, interpreted it as Venus crowning Mars.

13. Cubicle (g), S wall, central section: the painting with Polyphemus and Galatea is known to us from the pencil reproduction by G. Discanno (cfr. Disegnatori, p. 864, fig. 36), executed in 1873. Galatea, seen from behind and completely naked with the exception of her legs covered by the yellow mantle that has slipped off her, embraces Polyphemus, leaning against a rock. It is a replica of the same subject from the House of the Ancient Hunt VII 4, 48 (cf. vol. VII, p. 39, fig. 54), of which we have only the hatched reproduction that gives the impression of a rather clumsy composition and, at the time of discovery, poorly preserved, so much so that it is not defined in detail.

The protruding stucco frame is preserved only in the lower part with tabs, but it was much thicker judging by the position of the holes of the fixing nails.

15. Cubicle (g), S wall, section O: detail of the end of the architectural foreshortening with a black background with a simple curved wooden structure in front of which a vegetable candelabrum surmounted by a globe is placed.

16. Cubicle (g), S wall, section O: detail of the black plinth crossed by a carpet border with two parallel lines and with a central panel with long acroterial palmettes seen in profile, among flowering plants.

19. Cubicle (h): the fourth style decoration, defined as "very simple" by the Baron (GdS, II, 1870, c.9), has a red plinth and the middle area with panels and compartments now completely discolored.

The degradation of the plaster and the restoration work on the floors also prevent us from verifying this statement. 79 N54276

22. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E: the wall had a symmetrical structure with a central aedicule separated from the side panels by architectural views on a white background. The panel preserved in section E has a red background and is crossed by plant candelabra very close to those of the Temple of Isis, VIII 7, 28 and the House of the Vettii, VI 15,1; of the architectural foreshortening it is only possible to grasp the depiction of a pavilion in perspective. A polychrome stucco frame with vertical lotus buds and trefoils closes the composition at the top.
23. Tablinum (i), N wall, section E: detail of the side panel with a red background crossed by a vegetable candelabrum with corollas.

25. Tablinum (i), wall E, central section: detail of the vignette placed under the central aedicule. On the white background is depicted a sacred door with the usual tree with sparse leafy branches on the back.
27. Tablinum (i), wall E, section S: detail of the vignette in the red side panel. A bird resting on a flat is facing left.

Tablinum (i), wall E, section N of the lunette: figs protrude from the basket resting on the left, protected, as is still customary, by their own leaves, followed by the brightly colored rooster pecking at the large berries of a bunch of black grapes. Figs are also purple, which corresponds to the adjective pullus that Macrobius gives them when he enumerates among the known species of figs the Herculanea and the pulla Pompeiana, as noted in the commentary on this painting by C. Barone (GdS, II, 1870, c. 8).

29. Tablinum (i), wall E, section S of the lunette: the inverted basket is of a truncated conical shape different from that of the other which seems hemispherical; next to the grapes you can recognize two pomegranates, another typical fruit of the Vesuvius area. In this regard, it is worth mentioning the discovery of a considerable quantity of pomegranates left to ripen among the mats, in the Villa of L. Crassius Tertius in Oplontis during the excavations of the recent 80s. The bundle resting on the base has been defined by Trendelenburg as "of cereals", and by the Baron "of grass that is not well distinguished", it could therefore be unripe ears of corn or rather a bunch of asparagus that recurs several times in Pompeian still lifes, for example in the House of the Vettii, VI 15, 1 (see vol. V,  p. 538, figs. 118) or in the Temple of Isis, VIII 7, 28.
30. Tablinum (i), SE corner: detail of the stucco cornices of the lunette, with hanging trefoils and lotus buds and stylized palmettes circumscribed on an alternately red background O aZZUuIro.

Tablinum (i), S wall: the plinth, preserved for a short stretch, has a black background; in the middle area an architectural glimpse with a white background crossed by a candelabra, separates the red panel with floral candelabra from the one with a white background with very slender metal lateral candelabra around which they wrap to join in the center of the short sides, thin shoots with leaves.

32. Tablinum (i), vault, section N: in the decoration with a concentric structure a large part of the decorative repertoire of the IV style is organically used. From carpet borders, to garlands, to branches, from candelabras to thymiatéria, from medallions to ansati squares, from birds in flight to cupids. On the kidneys we find from E a corolla inserted in a half lozenge described by a border of a carpet in semicircles, a rectangle consisting of edges of a rectangular carpet supported by volutes and containing a picture with sea monsters. The large border follows towards the center with shoots connected to a small picture with a hippocampus, supported by a floral candelabrum and supporting a metal vase, and to a large thymiatérion that rests on a painting with a bird on a plane and is continued by the eagle in the central panel. In the corner towards wall E is the medallion with fawn, connected to arched garlands that depart from the outer band with the edges of a rectangular carpet with short curved sides.
33. Tablinum (i), vault, section N: detail of the painting with griffin and sea lion swimming to the left followed by a dolphin.
34. Tablinum (i), vault, N-W section: detail of the painting with a bird holding two cherries in its beak.

35. Tablinum (i), vault, section N-E: detail of the ansata table with a sea goat swimming to the left, supported by a floral candelabrum and supporting a metal cynochòe on which a red cloth is placed.

1. View of the external wall of the house from the secondary entrance at number 15 to the corner of the insula. The walls in opus incerta, in which there were restoration interventions with brick filling, especially in the E section, preserve the evident traces of the presence of an upper floor in the openings at the top and in the terracotta pipes for water disposal. On the high protruding plinth in red cocciopesto and on the middle area, which now appears in rough plaster, various electoral exhortations, painted and graffitied in favor of a Balbus, probably Q. Brittius Balbus, were read.

2. Vestibule (a): a papier-mâché floor with regular rows of crosses with a white centre and a border consisting of a row of white tesserae placed side by side, dating back to the first half of the first century BC.

The O wall, better preserved, allows you to recognize the architecture of the upper area.

Two moments of the myth that took place in different places and times are depicted on different registers. Above we see the hero who on the back of Pegasus pursues, with the spear menacingly brandished, the Chimera fleeing between the mountain crags. The small size of the figures gives the impression of distance from the scene depicted below, in an atmosphere of external calm but of intimate torment manifested above all on Stenebea's face. The queen, seated on a k&ne with a handmaid, welcomes Bellerophon who has returned victorious from his trial with the monstrous animal. The young man wearing a red chlamys edged with blue, is narrating the difficulties and dangers overcome and, while his outstretched hand seems a gesture of accusation towards the queen, her expression seems to suggest repentance for the false accusations made against the hero and the omen of approaching death. As narrated in Euripides' tragedy Stenebea (E fr. 664), from which the subject of the painting is probably taken, Bellerophon, pretending to have surrendered to the queen's love, will convince her to get on the winged horse to go to his kingdom of Caria but, having arrived on the island of Melo, he will throw it into the sea. In an airy mountain landscape where there is a small rural sanctuary with a small temple and sacred door, Paris, recognizable by his typically Phrygian clothing, which in the original was brightly colored, takes care of the flock that grazes and drinks from a stream that descends from the rocks and widens into a pool. Beyond this, two female figures sit on a rock (?) and the one on the left, diademated, points the young man to the girl who has her head veiled and further hides her face and in her hands holds a long peacock feather. It is clearly Aphrodite who persuades Helen to conquer Paris, still unaware of the fate that awaits him. The two moments, close together in a single setting, actually take place in different places and moments since when Paris meets Helen in Laconia he will have already abandoned pastoral life. The peacock feather that made Brizio believe it should be a heroine connected to that bird, for which he had proposed to interpret the scene as Taos convinced by Hera to love Argo, is instead most likely, as noted by Sogliano, only the index of Elena's extraordinary beauty.

Wing (8), black and white mosaic floor: the carpet is adorned with a network of laced octagons, a decorative motif that also appears in the cocciopesto and can be dated to the imperial age (IV style). In the sections adjacent to the walls, the marginal flounce is made of white tesserae arranged in an oblique warp; the warp is instead straight in the sections tangent to the marble thresholds towards the atrium (2) and the triclinium (16). In PAH, Il, p. 464 (17 May 1847) it is recorded that "H.R.H. honoured these Royal excavations the Crown Prince of Bavaria, wishing to observe the floors of the House of the Musicians,..., and they cleaned the floors of the right wing, and of the triclinium from the lapillus that covered them": as we read so many times in the reports of the time, the rooms had therefore been 'prepared',  so that the discovery could be quickly completed in the presence of some personalities visiting the excavations.
